title: Observed annual flow cut later runoff error, but recursive history had no clear gain at 188 south-east Australian catchments in 2010-2021
abstract: Can useful annual runoff history explain the persistent post-1997 runoff deficit? We fitted weather-only and weather-plus-previous-flow ridge models before 1997 at 188 south-east Australian catchments. We then supplied the same measured weather to two runs of each lag model. One run used observed previous flow; the other used its own previous prediction, with no later flow reset. In 2010-2021, observed history cut normalized squared error by 6.68% (conditional 95% limits 2.12 to 10.13) with annual weather controls and 3.76% (0.22 to 5.98) with detailed controls. Recursive history gave 0.04% (-2.09 to 1.98) and 0.48% (-1.64 to 1.92). Recursive runoff stayed 17.40% and 17.90% below prediction, relative to the pre-1997 mean. Observed history reduced these deficits by only 1.55 and 0.65 percentage points. Complete daily-flow, nonnegative, fixed-penalty, mainland and square-root checks retained the paired distinction. A fixed linear identity shows how observed flow can pass an unexplained deficit into the next prediction. Thus the tested flow-history skill does not provide a climate-driven simulation of the persistent loss. This result concerns two annual regularized model forms. It cannot exclude long physical storage memory or identify the cause. Short records, related gauges, source errors and conditional uncertainty limit inference. Code, exact source hashes, aggregate uncertainty samples, independent solver and information-flow audits, and a raw-source repeat are supplied. External records stay outside the bundle.
